name: Manganese toxicity / high-manganese response
summary: A Cannabis high-manganese treatment response reported as lower-leaf marginal chlorosis progressing inward to necrosis. The published treatment did not establish a universal toxic tissue threshold, so analytical context is required.
indicators: Marginal yellowing begins on lower leaves
Yellowing expands inward toward the midrib
Advanced leaves become severely chlorotic with necrotic margins and may abscise
Root-zone or tissue evidence supports elevated manganese exposure
exclusions: No elevated manganese exposure or tissue evidence exists
Boron toxicity, potassium deficiency, salinity, or root stress better explains marginal injury
Lesions are discrete and pathogen-like rather than exposure-distributed

progression.description: Chlorosis moves inward across the leaf surface.
Margins become necrotic, severe chlorosis develops, and some affected leaves may fall.

confirmation: Measure root-zone pH and manganese exposure and use tissue analysis when possible.
Do not use the 47.88 mg/kg value from one cultivar as a universal toxicity threshold; the authors specifically noted it fell within a prior survey range.
immediateActions: Verify pH, EC, fertilizer composition, source water, and tissue manganese before correction.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured manganese source or pH condition rather than treating leaf color alone.
Follow new growth and analytical values after correction.
prevention: Track micronutrient formulation and root-zone pH.
Use cultivar- and system-aware tissue interpretation.
warnings: The 2019 study found no significant biomass difference at the reported treatment and called for higher-concentration work to refine toxicity thresholds.
Visual marginal chlorosis is not manganese-specific.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

Manganese-toxicity plants developed marginal yellowing of lower leaves progressing inward, marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional abscission, but the measured Mn concentration remained within a previously published survey range and biomass did not differ significantly from controls.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.
